subject: Population-level priors for constrained individual-level parameters - what to truncate

messages.author: 73c3477df3617a0f
messages.subject: Population-level priors for constrained individual-level parameters - what to truncate
parts:
Hi,

After reading Ben's FAQ on truncated priors, I am still confused about how to apply truncation in multilevel models to avoid having prior probability mass outside of the parameter range.

My data is a series of Bernoulli choice trials using a logit link. Individuals have two parameters, k and c, which define their choice evaluation (k) and consistency (c). At the population level, individual k's come from a lognormal distribution and individual c's come from a normal distribution. I want to constrain each individual's c to be above some lower bound, e.g. 0.25. The reason is that if c's can be negative or very small, corresponding k's become weakly identifiable and some don't converge. When I put a constraint on c's, what (if anything) do I have to truncate on the priors for parameters that describe the population-level distribution of c's?

Thank you for your help; my code is below. Suggested alternatives to a hard constraint on c also welcome.

Erin

//model.stan (also attached)
data{
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> N_subject;
  int<lower=0, upper=1> ssr[N];//outcome being modeled with Bernoulli trials
  real AmountNow[N];
  real AmountLater[N];
  real DelayNow[N];
  real DelayLater[N];
  int subj_index[N];
  real age_c[N_subject]; //mean centered age
}

parameters{
  vector<lower=0>[N_subject] k; //each subject has a k that determines their decision process
  vector<lower=0.25> [N_subject] c;//individual consistency c has a lower bound at .25
  real mu_logK; //center of the lognormal distribution of k's
  real<lower=0> sigma_logK; //variance of the lognormal distribution of k's
  real b_age;//effect of age on logK
  real<lower=0> sigma_c;//variance of normal distribution of c's
  real mu_c;//IS A CONSTRAINT <lower=0.25> NEEDED because individual c's are constrained > 0.25?
  real c_age;//effect of age on consistency c
}

model{
  vector[N] v;
  vector[N_subject] c_mid;
  vector[N_subject] logK_mid;
  mu_c ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//MY Q: IS TRUNCATION NEEDED HERE TOO T[ 0.25, ] because individual c's are bounded below by 0.25?
  sigma_c ~ exponential( 2 );
  c_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//prior for effect of age on c. DO I NEED TO WORRY ABOUT THIS TERM BRINGING c_mid < 0.25
  b_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 ); //prior for effect of age on logK
  sigma_logK ~ exponential( 2 );
  mu_logK ~ normal( 0 , 10 );
  for (n in 1:N_subject) {//age offset to means of c and logK
    c_mid[n] <- mu_c + c_age * age_c[n];
    logK_mid[n] <- mu_logK + b_age * age_c[n];
  }
  c ~ normal( c_mid , sigma_c ) T[ 0.25, ];//This is what I understood was necessary from the FAQ on truncated priors
  k ~ lognormal( logK_mid , sigma_logK ); //theory suggests k's are distributed lognormal across individuals.
  
  for ( i in 1:N ) {
    v[i] <- c[subj_index[i]]*( AmountNow[i] / ( 1 + k[subj_index[i]] * DelayNow[i] ) ) - 
    ( AmountLater[i] / ( 1 + k[subj_index[i]] * DelayLater[i] ) ); 
    //v is the subjective difference between amounts multiplied by an individual's consistency scaling term, c
  }
  
  ssr ~ bernoulli_logit( v );//probability dist. is Bernoulli for each choice
}

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Population-level priors for constrained individual-level parameters - what to truncate
parts:
On Saturday, August 27, 2016 at 2:06:49 AM UTC-4, ErinC wrote:
After reading Ben's FAQ on truncated priors, I am still confused about how to apply truncation in multilevel models to avoid having prior probability mass outside of the parameter range.

Truncation is not wrong. Lack of truncation is wrong if you truncate away a non-constant amount of area. Truncation is slow, so we avoid it when truncating away a constant amount of area. Truncation won't help if there is posterior density on the truncation point because that is negative infinity in the unconstrained space. So you are probably better off taking your chances without the constraint and a prior that does not put much density on values that are too low.
real mu_c;//IS A CONSTRAINT <lower=0.25> NEEDED because individual c's are constrained > 0.25?
Yes, if you keep that 0.25 constraint on c.
mu_c ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//MY Q: IS TRUNCATION NEEDED HERE TOO T[ 0.25, ] because individual c's are bounded below by 0.25?
The area to the left of 0.25 under a standard normal is a constant.
c_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//prior for effect of age on c. DO I NEED TO WORRY ABOUT THIS TERM BRINGING c_mid < 0.25
Yes.
c ~ normal( c_mid , sigma_c ) T[ 0.25, ];//This is what I understood was necessary from the FAQ on truncated priors

because the area to the left of 0.25 is not constant.

Ben

- What do you mean by truncation 'won't help' if there is posterior density on the truncation point? Should I be getting numerical errors if this happens or will my posterior be wrong without stan error messages?
So you are probably better off taking your chances without the constraint and a prior that does not put much density on values that are too low.

- Are you suggesting I use more informative priors for mu_c and sigma_c or change the type of prior I use for the population distribution (I'm not sure what a reasonable alternative is to a truncated normal(c_mid, sigma_c))?

real mu_c;//IS A CONSTRAINT <lower=0.25> NEEDED because individual c's are constrained > 0.25?

Yes, if you keep that 0.25 constraint on c.
 
  mu_c ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//MY Q: IS TRUNCATION NEEDED HERE TOO T[ 0.25, ] because individual c's are bounded below by 0.25?

The area to the left of 0.25 under a standard normal is a constant.
 
  c_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//prior for effect of age on c. DO I NEED TO WORRY ABOUT THIS TERM BRINGING c_mid < 0.25

Yes. - What can I do about this? It's not clear to me how to constrain c_age to ensure c_mid stays within [ 0.25, ] since age (age_c for centered) is a continuous variable. I'd like to eventually also add in an additional predictor, which adds challenge.

messages.subject: Re: Population-level priors for constrained individual-level parameters - what to truncate
parts:
On Sunday, August 28, 2016 at 5:18:29 PM UTC-4, ErinC wrote:
- What do you mean by truncation 'won't help' if there is posterior density on the truncation point? Should I be getting numerical errors if this happens or will my posterior be wrong without stan error messages?
Probably will get a lot of divergent transitions

So you are probably better off taking your chances without the constraint and a prior that does not put much density on values that are too low.
- Are you suggesting I use more informative priors for mu_c and sigma_c or change the type of prior I use for the population distribution (I'm not sure what a reasonable alternative is to a truncated normal(c_mid, sigma_c))?
If 0.25 is more than 2 or 3 sigma_c units from c_mid, then it will rarely be down to 0.25 but not require a transformation 0.25 + exp(...).

c_age ~ normal( 0 , 1 );//prior for effect of age on c. DO I NEED TO WORRY ABOUT THIS TERM BRINGING c_mid < 0.25

Yes. - What can I do about this? It's not clear to me how to constrain c_age to ensure c_mid stays within [ 0.25, ] since age (age_c for centered) is a continuous variable. I'd like to eventually also add in an additional predictor, which adds challenge.

It is very difficult. You have to store the max and min of age_c in transformed data and then choose bounds on mu_c such that c_age * min_age is small enough when c_age > 0 and c_age * max_age is small enough when c_age > 0.

Ben
